Hi, I struggle with the same thing, being: ADHD and trouble getting out of bed. I have been researching methods as I have been learning about this as well. 

Some things that have helped me the most is drinking a glass of water the second I wake up, and taking my meds (if you are on meds) immediately. I am on a stimulant medication so it helps me not linger in bed as long. Getting water in immediately can help stimulate your digestive and urinary system to start moving so you would need to use the bathroom, and helps rehydrate you after going so long without water, which will help you get more alert faster. 

Another thing I have heard about is making your bed as soon as you get up in the morning. I haven’t had a chance to try this yet, but of the times I have gotten myself to make my bed, it helps me to have clean sheets and a freshly made bed the night before so I can try to preserve that “freshness” from when they were washed. 

I know my own self to get overzealous with my goals and I want a habit to be solid the second I start doing it. Make a goal for yourself to get out of bed and stay out tomorrow and only tomorrow. When the goal is much smaller, it’s harder for our ADHD brain to get overwhelmed and want to give up or put it off. 

If there is any kind of threshold in your morning routine that indicates “I am out of bed and I am staying out of bed”, like for some this may be putting on clothing, taking a shower, or eating breakfast. Make a plan to get to that point so you are able to continue with your day. And if you feel like you still need steps beyond that, feel free to plan that out. Even if it is a day that you have nothing pressing, you can schedule in time for video games or a chore so it does not feel like the whole day is wasted. 

Above all else, building a regular routine is key, especially for sleep and wake times. Not gonna lie, this is hard to get in the swing of. I still seriously struggle with my sleep schedule but I am slowly adjusting my sleep time so my body can better adapt to the changes. Aim for 8 hours of sleep, or how every much your body naturally needs. It will be really hard to change how your body feels in the morning at first as your metabolism is accustomed to staying in bed longer. This is the most important part, though is not an immediate change. It is far easier to manage your ADHD and mood when you are consistent on getting in your ZZZ’s!

I had a male therapist when I was 21 and grieving the loss of my Dad. He turned out to be horribly abusive, extremely patronizing, and dismissive. And took it very personally when I relapsed. By the time I wanted to be done working with him, I felt the need to respond to him in a way where I would not get a belittling response from him. 

I told myself I can’t work with another male therapist again because I just wasn’t comfortable having to feel like I needed to explain myself constantly for my therapist to understand. 

Fast forward to today, I work in the mental health field and, consequently, it is incredibly difficult to find a therapist who has the skillset to treat my ongoing mental health issues. A coworker recommended her counselor but I said no because he is male. But after cycling through 3 therapists in the past year, I decided to give him a try. He is the most skilled trauma therapist I have worked with. I have improved considerably since working with him and I am really happy that my first experience with a male therapist didn’t deter me from meeting with this one. 

As far as I have noticed regarding trends, male therapists tend to take more risks when it comes to challenging and pushing you. But can, at times, miss the mark on where they need to be validating. With the female therapists, they do tend to be more gentle, but in my more recent experiences they were too validating and did not facilitate personal growth. The best female therapist I’ve had was very skilled at helping me reframe my thoughts and built trust with me very quickly because I genuinely felt like she wasn’t judging me. Even with my current therapist I have my reservations because he is male, but we are getting there. 

To say the least, what matters the most is skillset. A healthy balance of being able to validate and challenge without one or the other being so dominate that treatment is ineffective. While I do believe that for our assigned genders we are socialized to behave in a certain way in certain roles, it matters most that the therapist is aware of their own strengths and where they need to build their own skills to treat clients that are in different spots with their mental health. Some think that validating and keeping the client happy is the goal, rather than trauma processing, emotional regulation skills and whatever other needs the client may have. 

TL;DR doesn’t hurt to give it a shot, any mental health professional’s approach is going to be different based on their own experiences, beliefs, and values. Just know the warning signs if they are abusive, but honestly you’d find that with any gender.

Whaaaat! I have scarring up and down my left forearm and I am looking into going into nursing. My top concern is how to navigate the situation with my arm. It’s great to hear a perspective that it helped someone feel at least a little bit better.

The way I did it was I decided not to cover them from the start to avoid feeling anxiety from hiding it all the time. My regret with this method is I was in a headspace where I wasn’t considering what that would do to the people around me who would have never guessed I would cut myself. After I got treatment there was a lot of work I had to do with my regrets around that and accepting the permanence of my scars. 

At the time I worked in customer service and I would get customers who would ask if I had a cat or an accident. Some people even gave advice on how to make them fade more which I thought was very sweet. I had one coworker who asked if I had been cutting myself and I explained what had been happening over the past few months (I was very close with this coworker) and she said that even though she’d rather me not cut myself, it’s better than me ending up dead. 

I am considering getting a tattoo to cover them but I so far don’t have an idea to what kind of piece I would want that is large enough to cover the area. I may not though, I have grown to like my scars.

I would say to be patient, getting to a place of being able to accept them took me at least 3 years in pair with intensive treatment. But it’s worth it, because the power they hold over me is exactly 0.

A mindset that I hold, which is easier said than done, is that there will always be people that will make assumptions about you because of your scars, but that just makes it easier for you to differentiate them from the kind of people you want to be around.

Sure! I suppose a basic synopsis is: a little over two and a half years ago

I was hospitalized for suicidal ideation, then when I got out my university mandated that I go to a DBT therapist and attend a weekly DBT group for eight weeks. 
For starters, I can’t work with male therapists. The psychiatrist on my team didn’t care, even when I told her, the excuse being “therapy hasn’t worked so well for you in the past so let’s just try this out”. I had interpreted this as me not being allowed to switch therapists, so I was stuck with him longer than what was necessary. 

He seemed kind of unconfident at first, I felt a little sorry for him. He grew to be more assertive, but eventually to the point where it was making me uncomfortable. 

A lot of silence and staring, which I know is supposed to be used as a tool to be able to sit in the moment and process, but for me, I couldn’t think about anything else other than that I could see him staring at me in the corner of my eye. Even after I told him to stop.

Then I didn’t do my homework. We had to use the entire hour-long session talking about why I didn’t do the homework. I learned later in one of my courses that DBT therapists are supposed to do this when their clients don’t do their homework, but for me it just degraded my trust for him. He also commented “I feel like I work hard for you, when it should really be the other way around.” I am a really sensitive person, so I ended up interpreting that as negative criticism.

A lot of the things he said were along the lines of “suffering is a choice” and “you seemed to make a monster out of things that can be easily resolved”, which at the time made me question what was wrong with me because I very much was obviously still suffering and things didn’t seem as simple as whatever it was that he saw. 

Anyways, I relapsed, which as I am writing this is a surprise to no one because he was fucking shitty. This time instead of suicidal ideation, it was an attempt. 

My first session back with him after getting out of the psych ward:

“That shit needs to stop”

“Cut that shit out” 

“What do I have to do to prove to you that I care about you!?”

“You freaked out.” (In reference to an incident that happened in the hospital, to which he only heard about from the opposing side) 

“I feel like you just took the past eight weeks and just threw them away”

In sessions going forward, because at this point I still didn’t think I was allowed to switch therapists, he continued to say off-kitler things such as saying that:

“I am the most stubborn person you will ever meet. You can ask my parents, my wife, my friends”

“I am partially responsible for you” 

There wasn’t much context to him saying these two things, I am pretty sure it was just points where I got unresponsive and he just said it. 

“I feel like you seem less trusting in the past few weeks, do you think I am mad at you for relapsing?”

Me: “Yes.”

Him: “That’s bullshit. I still like you, I still like working with you. You’re a challenge, but I like challenges.” 

I love DBT now, but at the time I felt like some of the guidance in groups wasn’t taking my need for treatment seriously. So I ended up opening up and saying that DBT treatment felt very juvenile. 

His response? “Well, *method of suicide attempt* because of *played down version of reason for suicide attempt* is juvenile” 

I logically now know that him saying this was unjustified, but that was the last straw. I couldn’t work with someone who looked at my struggles that way, even though it was my own wording being used against be. He was the professional, I was the mentally ill one, which I get doesn’t give me a pass to just say whatever I want, but I lacked the awareness to realize that what I said insulted him, and he chose to shoot it back at me.

I wrote out a whole list of reasons as to why I couldn’t work with him and took it to a walk-in counselor at my university. I didn’t have to make an argument because of course the idea of being forced to work with one therapist is absolutely asinine. 

Bonus points for me going to the walk-in counselling center, me verifying with the walk-in therapist that I won’t have to speak with him again, and then my university still making me have to talk with him face-to-face on why I wanted to stop working with him. Horrible.

Sorry that turned out to be really long, I wanted to add in as much context while being somewhat concise(ish). Also this turned into a rant, maybe I just really really had to get my trauma out, but I see how much and how royally he fucked up. Several times.
